title: Al-Ghaffar, the Ever-Forgiving
tomorrow: the wall needs a sign-off Amira can't get. now what?

cards: The third sorry text in one week weighs more than the first. By then it can feel like the word has worn out. Yesterday's question was Amira's: how many sorries still count?
There's a hadith about exactly that, and it repeats itself on purpose, like a refrain.

teach.h: A SERVANT ASKS, AND ASKS AGAIN.
teach.b: In Bukhari's collection, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, tells of a servant who commits a sin and says: my Lord, forgive me.
In paraphrase, Allah says: My servant knew he has a Lord who forgives sins and holds to account for them. I have forgiven him. Then the servant sins again, and asks again, and the same answer comes.
And again. The refrain is the point.

That's today's name, al-Ghaffar, the Ever-Forgiving: the forgiving that doesn't run out on the second or third return. The Qur'an says it plainly: "Despair not of the mercy of Allah, Who forgiveth all sins."
The tradition also attaches forgiveness to something you can feel.
A hadith in Sahih Muslim says that when a believer makes wudu, the washing before prayer, the wrongs of the hands and the eyes leave with the water, with its last drop.
Water you can feel on your wrists, carrying something you can't see.
Here's what to tell a friend tonight: in this hadith, coming back for the third time isn't the failure. Stopping coming back would be. The asking still has to be real, and the fault is still a fault.
But the door the servant knocks on doesn't lock after a set number of knocks.

how: Muslims ask forgiveness with words like astaghfirullah, and hadith link forgiveness with wudu, the washing before prayer.

o: the One who forgives, and forgives again
the One who forgives only a first mistake
the One who forgets each wrong at once

games.q: the servant who returns — tap the pairs.

s: forgiveness runs out if you repeat the same sin
in the hadith the servant returns again and again, and the answer each time is: I have forgiven him.
the Qur'an says despair not of the mercy of Allah
despair not of the mercy of Allah, Who forgiveth all sins.
being forgiven again means the fault no longer matters
the asking has to be real, and the fault is still a fault. the door just doesn't lock.

games.q: the servant in the hadith has sinned a second time. what does the story have him do next?
o: ask his Lord again, and hear the same answer: forgiven.
stay away, since asking twice for the same thing is shameless.
make up for it alone first, and only ask once it's fixed.
games.why: he asks again, and the reply repeats: my servant knew he has a Lord who forgives. the refrain is the teaching.

practice: If water is close, let it run over your hands, slowly: the cool on your wrists, the weight across the palms, then the last drop leaving a fingertip; if not, rest your hands open on your knees and feel the air on them.

While the sit runs, bring to mind one fault you keep repeating, the same one, not a new one. If you pray, you can say astaghfirullah, I ask God's forgiveness, the words Muslims use, softly, once with each slow breath.
If you don't, name the fault to yourself without arguing for it, and let each out-breath be the water leaving your hands.

wordCard.voice: Al-Ghaffar: the Ever-Forgiving, who forgives the one who returns, and the one who returns again.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: again and again, for as long as the asking is real. Day done.
